messages.subject: Q on occu with TMB engine for random effects
messages.subject_clean: Q on occu with TMB engine for random effects
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I just wanted to try out the cool new TMB engine in unmarked to fit a static occupancy model (i.e., with function 'occu') that has a random effect of year. Mine is a small data set with 51 sites x 3 replicates and collected over 3 years. As a first attempt at a random-effects occupancy model I wanted to declare the winter as a random-effects factor in the detection model and did this:

(fmX <- occu(~ (1 | winter) ~1, data = umf))

R crashed on this. Did I do anything silly ? I know that a random-effects factor with only 3 levels is a bit questionable, but it should not be technically wrong to fit such a model.

Thanks and best regards -- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Hello team,

I'm running a single season single species occupancy model, but my null model keeps giving the error 'Hessian is singular'. Naive occupancy for the species is fairly high (ranging between 0.26 to 0.65). I tried following some previous threads, but have been unable to solve the issue. I haven't had this issue when I've run very similar models for a different season.

umf <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y= fox_det[,37:71],
                         siteCovs = veg_combined_postfire[,c('veg20_50cm','treatment','burn','canopy','edge_dist')],
                         obsCovs = NULL)

null <-occu(~1~1,data=umf)

Giving starts= c(1,0) gives me this:

Any help would be much appreciated, thanks a lot!

Regards,
Vishnu

messages.body_plain:
Dear Vishnu,
 you're getting a singular Hessian warning there because the MLE is on the boundary of the parameter space (psi = 1). Sadly, your two-dimensional likelihood lives only in one dimension.
 The good news is you can use a logistic regression to study the variables that affect detection probability!
regards
andy

messages.body_plain:
Dear Ken, all,

exploring the TMB-mediated random-effects option in unmarked a little more I discovered this: apparently, as soon as we add a random-effects factor in the detection model, then ALL covariates specified in the detection model must be of the obsCov format. In my unmarked data frame, 'method' is an obsCov, 'datum' is a siteCov and 'obsDatum' is the obsCov variant of 'datum'. Here's the behaviour of unmarked for three models using these explanatory variables:

(fmX <- occu(~methode+datum-1 ~1, data = umf))  # Works

(fmX <- occu(~methode+datum-1 + (1 | obsWinter) ~1, data = umf))

# does not work, yields the following error:

Error in model.frame.default(lme4::subbars(formula), data, na.action = stats::na.pass) :
  variable lengths differ (found for 'datum')

(fmX <- occu(~methode+obsDatum-1 + (1 | obsWinter) ~1, data = umf)) # does work

That's no big deal, but we just have to remember to create 'clones' as obsCovs for all covariates that we intend to use in the detection model when any random-effects factor is also present.

Thanks again and best regards  -- Marc

messages.subject: Q on predictions for occu with TMB engine for random effects
messages.subject_clean: Q on predictions for occu with TMB engine for random effects
messages.body_plain:
Dear Ken,

I am stranded when trying to form predictions for my static occupancy model which in p has one fixed-effect factor ('methode') with three levels, plus a random-effects factor ('transekt') with 49 levels. This is for a survey where a total of 180 bridges that are nested in transects were surveyed for otter sign by three types of persons ('experts', 'otterspotters', 'dog'). My fitted model is summarized as follows:

Call:
occu(formula = ~(methode - 1) + (1 | transekt) ~ 1, data = umf)

Occupancy:
 Estimate    SE    z P(>|z|)

    0.667 0.268 2.49  0.0128

Detection:
Random effects:
   Groups        Name Variance Std.Dev.

 transekt (Intercept)   17.944    4.236

Fixed effects:
                    Estimate   SE     z P(>|z|)

methodeexpertin        -3.91 1.34 -2.91 0.00363
methodehund            -1.77 1.21 -1.46 0.14343
methodeotterspotter    -4.48 1.38 -3.25 0.00115

AIC: 348.4884

How can I predict the fixed effects (i.e., for 'methode'), while accommodating the uncertainty due to the random transect ? I tried the following, which had worked in the model without the random transekt effects, but this now throws an error:
predict(fm5, "det", newdat = data.frame(methode = c('expertin', 'otterspotter', 'hund')))
Error in eval(predvars, data, env) : object 'transekt' not found

Adding the transect factor in the data.frame for which we predict does produce output, but returns a prediction for every single one of the 180 bridges in the data set.
predict(fm5, "det", newdat = data.frame(methode = rep(c('expertin', 'otterspotter', 'hund'), 180), transekt = umf@obsCovs$transekt[1:180]))

Thanks for your help and best regards  -- Marc

messages.subject: Re: Q on predictions for occu with TMB engine for random effects
messages.subject_clean: Q on predictions for occu with TMB engine for random effects
messages.body_plain:
Marc,

You can exclude the random effects component from the prediction by setting the argument re.form=NA:

predict(fm5, "det", newdat = data.frame(methode = c('expertin', 'otterspotter', 'hund')), re.form=NA)

However I'm not sure if this is "accommodating the uncertainty in the random transect" by your definition since the uncertainty in the random effects estimates will not be reflected in the uncertainty intervals around the predictions for each level of method. Only the uncertainty in the fixed effect parameters.

You could generate predictions for a specific transect, which is similar to what you did:

predict(fm5, "det", newdat = data.frame(methode = c('expertin', 'otterspotter', 'hund'), transkect="A"))

This at least incorporates the uncertainty in the estimate of the random effect for transect A when generating the uncertainty for the prediction. However I believe it is not accounting for uncertainty in the variance parameters. It is possible to get from TMB a full covariance matrix including all parameters (fixed and random) so perhaps I should implement some kind of bootstrapping approach to getting the CIs.

Ken

Thanks for your reply, that makes sense. This might be a silly question- but why is the standard error so high when psi is almost 1 and given that the naive occ is high?

Regards,
Vishnu

On Tuesday, November 2, 2021 at 11:35:07 AM UTC+11 Jeffrey Royle wrote:
> Dear Vishnu,
>  you're getting a singular Hessian warning there because the MLE is on the boundary of the parameter space (psi = 1). Sadly, your two-dimensional likelihood lives only in one dimension.
>  The good news is you can use a logistic regression to study the variables that affect detection probability!
> regards
> andy
>
>

> > Hello team,
> >
> > I'm running a single season single species occupancy model, but my null model keeps giving the error 'Hessian is singular'. Naive occupancy for the species is fairly high (ranging between 0.26 to 0.65). I tried following some previous threads, but have been unable to solve the issue. I haven't had this issue when I've run very similar models for a different season.

General curiosity question -- I see (I think...) that results from TMB models (e.g, below) include a calculated AIC. Since AIC for random effects models has only been fully vetted for RE based on method-of-moments (sensu Ken Burnham), was wondering how the AIC (like the one shown below) is calculated? I've used Watanabe-Akaike (WAIC) for some RE models in a different context, but other than Ken Burnham's MoM approach, I've seen no concensus opinion on AIC for anything other than likelihood-based models.

On 11/2/2021 9:13 PM, unma...@googlegroups.com wrote:

> Q on occu with TMB engine for random effects  <http://groups.google.com/group/unmarked/t/c518a70e55b4dc85?utm_source=digest&utm_medium=email>
> Marc Kery <marc...@vogelwarte.ch>: Nov 02 08:26AM
>
> Dear Ken,
>
> fantastic, and yes, exactly. Winter is a site covariate. Creating a 'clone' in the format of an observational covariate worked like a charm.
>
> Call:
> occu(formula = ~(1 | obsWinter) ~ 1, data = umf)
>
> Occupancy:
> Estimate SE z P(>|z|)
> 0.482 0.323 1.49 0.136
>
> Detection:
> Random effects:
> Groups Name Variance Std.Dev.
> obsWinter (Intercept) 0.491 0.701
>
> Fixed effects:
> Estimate SE z P(>|z|)
> 1.13 0.546 2.08 0.0379
>
> AIC: 164.087
>
> Thanks for the quick help and especially also for making the random-effects option via TMB available in unmarked ! This is really a great addition to the package.
>
> Best regards --- Marc

> Dear all,

> I just wanted to try out the cool new TMB engine in unmarked to fit a static occupancy model (i.e., with function 'occu') that has a random effect of year. Mine is a small data set with 51 sites x 3 replicates and collected over 3 years. As a first attempt at a random-effects occupancy model I wanted to declare the winter as a random-effects factor in the detection model and did this:
>
>
> (fmX <- occu(~ (1 | winter) ~1, data = umf))

> Dear Ken, all,
>
> exploring the TMB-mediated random-effects option in unmarked a little more I discovered this: apparently, as soon as we add a random-effects factor in the detection model, then ALL covariates specified in the detection model must be of the obsCov format. In my unmarked data frame, 'method' is an obsCov, 'datum' is a siteCov and 'obsDatum' is the obsCov variant of 'datum'. Here's the behaviour of unmarked for three models using these explanatory variables:
>
>
> (fmX <- occu(~methode+datum-1 ~1, data = umf)) # Works
>
> (fmX <- occu(~methode+datum-1 + (1 | obsWinter) ~1, data = umf))
>
> # does not work, yields the following error:
>
> Error in model.frame.default(lme4::subbars(formula), data, na.action = stats::na.pass) :
> variable lengths differ (found for 'datum')
>
> (fmX <- occu(~methode+obsDatum-1 + (1 | obsWinter) ~1, data = umf)) # does work
>
> That's no big deal, but we just have to remember to create 'clones' as obsCovs for all covariates that we intend to use in the detection model when any random-effects factor is also present.
>
> Thanks again and best regards -- Marc

> Dear Ken,
>
> I am stranded when trying to form predictions for my static occupancy model which in p has one fixed-effect factor ('methode') with three levels, plus a random-effects factor ('transekt') with 49 levels. This is for a survey where a total of 180 bridges that are nested in transects were surveyed for otter sign by three types of persons ('experts', 'otterspotters', 'dog'). My fitted model is summarized as follows:
>
> Call:
> occu(formula = ~(methode - 1) + (1 | transekt) ~ 1, data = umf)
>
> Occupancy:
> Estimate SE z P(>|z|)
> 0.667 0.268 2.49 0.0128
>
> Detection:
> Random effects:
> Groups Name Variance Std.Dev.
> transekt (Intercept) 17.944 4.236
>
> Fixed effects:
> Estimate SE z P(>|z|)
> methodeexpertin -3.91 1.34 -2.91 0.00363
> methodehund -1.77 1.21 -1.46 0.14343
> methodeotterspotter -4.48 1.38 -3.25 0.00115
>
> AIC: 348.4884
>
> How can I predict the fixed effects (i.e., for 'methode'), while accommodating the uncertainty due to the random transect ? I tried the following, which had worked in the model without the random transekt effects, but this now throws an error:
> predict(fm5, "det", newdat = data.frame(methode = c('expertin', 'otterspotter', 'hund')))
> Error in eval(predvars, data, env) : object 'transekt' not found
>
> Adding the transect factor in the data.frame for which we predict does produce output, but returns a prediction for every single one of the 180 bridges in the data set.
> predict(fm5, "det", newdat = data.frame(methode = rep(c('expertin', 'otterspotter', 'hund'), 180), transekt = umf@obsCovs$transekt[1:180]))
>
> Thanks for your help and best regards -- Marc
> Ken Kellner <con...@kenkellner.com>: Nov 02 08:30AM -0700
>
> Marc,
>
> You can exclude the random effects component from the prediction by setting
> the argument re.form=NA:
>
> predict(fm5, "det", newdat = data.frame(methode = c('expertin',
> 'otterspotter', 'hund')), re.form=NA)
>
> However I'm not sure if this is "accommodating the uncertainty in the
> random transect" by your definition since the uncertainty in the random
> effects estimates will not be reflected in the uncertainty intervals around
> the predictions for each level of method. Only the uncertainty in the fixed
> effect parameters.
>
> You could generate predictions for a specific transect, which is similar to
> what you did:
>
> predict(fm5, "det", newdat = data.frame(methode = c('expertin',
> 'otterspotter', 'hund'), transkect="A"))
>
> This at least incorporates the uncertainty in the estimate of the random
> effect for transect A when generating the uncertainty for the prediction.
> However I believe it is not accounting for uncertainty in the variance
> parameters. It is possible to get from TMB a full covariance matrix
> including all parameters (fixed and random) so perhaps I should implement
> some kind of bootstrapping approach to getting the CIs.
>
> Ken
>

messages.body_plain:
It's calculated as 2*K - 2 * log(lik), where K is the number of fixed effect parameters + number of random effect variances. I used this method to emulate how package lme4 calculates AIC for mixed models. I'm certainly open to suggestions for taking a different approach.

Ken

On Tuesday, November 2, 2021 at 9:23:35 PM UTC-4 evan....@gmail.com wrote:
> General curiosity question -- I see (I think...) that results from TMB models (e.g, below) include a calculated AIC. Since AIC for random effects models has only been fully vetted for RE based on method-of-moments (sensu Ken Burnham), was wondering how the AIC (like the one shown below) is calculated? I've used Watanabe-Akaike (WAIC) for some RE models in a different context, but other than Ken Burnham's MoM approach, I've seen no concensus opinion on AIC for anything other than likelihood-based models.

> >
> > predict(fm5, "det", newdat = data.frame(methode = c('expertin',
> > 'otterspotter', 'hund')), re.form=NA)
> >
> > However I'm not sure if this is "accommodating the uncertainty in the
> > random transect" by your definition since the uncertainty in the random
> > effects estimates will not be reflected in the uncertainty intervals around
> > the predictions for each level of method. Only the uncertainty in the fixed
> > effect parameters.
> >
> > You could generate predictions for a specific transect, which is similar to
> > what you did:
> >
> > predict(fm5, "det", newdat = data.frame(methode = c('expertin',
> > 'otterspotter', 'hund'), transkect="A"))
> >
> > This at least incorporates the uncertainty in the estimate of the random
> > effect for transect A when generating the uncertainty for the prediction.
> > However I believe it is not accounting for uncertainty in the variance
> > parameters. It is possible to get from TMB a full covariance matrix
> > including all parameters (fixed and random) so perhaps I should implement
> > some kind of bootstrapping approach to getting the CIs.
> >
> > Ken

messages.body_plain:
Dear Evan,

and note that with TMB as an engine, unmarked is still doing maximum likelihood, that's the beauty.

Best regards  --- Marc

From: unma...@googlegroups.com <unma...@googlegroups.com> on behalf of Ken Kellner <con...@kenkellner.com>

Sent: Wednesday, November 3, 2021 03:19
To: unmarked <unma...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: Re: [unmarked] Digest for unma...@googlegroups.com - 5 updates in 1 topic

It's calculated as 2*K - 2 * log(lik), where K is the number of fixed effect parameters + number of random effect variances. I used this method to emulate how package lme4 calculates AIC for mixed models. I'm certainly open to suggestions for taking a different approach.

Ken

On Tuesday, November 2, 2021 at 9:23:35 PM UTC-4 evan....@gmail.com wrote:
> General curiosity question -- I see (I think...) that results from TMB models (e.g, below) include a calculated AIC. Since AIC for random effects models has only been fully vetted for RE based on method-of-moments (sensu Ken Burnham), was wondering how the AIC (like the one shown below) is calculated? I've used Watanabe-Akaike (WAIC) for some RE models in a different context, but other than Ken Burnham's MoM approach, I've seen no concensus opinion on AIC for anything other than likelihood-based models.

I wonder if the issue is about starting values.  If you try start=c(0.3, -3), do you get reasonable results?

I suspect that the estimate should not be on the border because the number of detections is greater than

> n*visits * (1 - (n0/n)^(1/v))

where n is the number of sites (147), v is the number of visits to each site (which seems to be pretty consistent at either 34 or 35 visits per site), and n0 is the number of sites with no detections (which is 147 - 70 = 77).  The number of detections is 145 and the above formula results in

>  147*35*(1-(77/147)^(1/35)) = 94.2

We have 145 > 94.2 and so the "real" maximum likelihood estimate shouldn't be 1.  (This formula works just for the model with no covariates.)

Jim

Here's an update on why I think it's just a matter of better starting values.  Below is a made-up dataset that matches all of the summary statistics you gave and gives almost identical results.  (I've compacted the dataset to take up much less space than listing out all of the elements.  That's why it looks so odd.)  But then using different starting values than what you used gives the correct results.

But more importantly:  you should follow Andy's advice about using logistic regression and not worrying about less-than-perfect detection for this dataset.  And I'd argue you want to use all of the sites for studying occupancy but just the sites with at least one detection to study the probability of detection using logistic regression.  If you choose to continue with occu, then trying multiple starting values would be essential and settling on the starting values giving you the smallest AIC value.  It appears that while the detection probability for an individual visit is low, you have typically 35 visits to each site and the probability of at least one detection in 35 visits is very close to 1.

y = matrix(c(1,1,1,1,1,rep(0,29),NA,1,1,1,1,1,rep(0,29),NA,1,1,1,1,rep(0,30),NA,
  rep(c(rep(0,34),NA),32),rep(c(1,1,rep(0,33)), 64),1,rep(0,34),1,rep(0,34),1,
  rep(0,1609)), nrow=147, byrow=TRUE)

ufo = unmarkedFrameOccu(y = y)
summary(ufo)
# unmarkedFrame Object
#
# 147 sites
# Maximum number of observations per site: 35
# Mean number of observations per site: 34.76
# Sites with at least one detection: 70
#
# Tabulation of y observations:
#    0    1 <NA>
# 4965  145   35

occu(~1 ~1, ufo, start=c(1,0))
# Call:
# occu(formula = ~1 ~ 1, data = ufo, starts = c(1, 0))
#
# Occupancy:
#  Estimate   SE      z P(>|z|)
#      20.8 1712 0.0122    0.99
#
# Detection:
#  Estimate     SE     z P(>|z|)
#     -3.53 0.0842 -41.9       0
#
# AIC: 1322.89

So the results match up pretty well with what you presented.  However, using different starting values gives one more reasonable (and I think correct) results:

occu(~1 ~1, ufo, start=c(0.3,-3))
# Call:
# occu(formula = ~1 ~ 1, data = ufo, starts = c(0.3, -3))
#
# Occupancy:
#  Estimate    SE   z P(>|z|)
#     0.316 0.225 1.4    0.16
#
# Detection:
#  Estimate    SE     z   P(>|z|)
#     -2.97 0.108 -27.5 2.34e-166
#
# AIC: 1286.282
   (
The moral is anytime you use a program dependent on iterative methods, be prepared to give reasonable (or multiple) starting values.  (This advice doesn't just apply to occu.)

Jim

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone, I hope you are all well.

I did a multi-species occupancy analysis in unmarked with 4 species. My top model included only one covariate for psi. Now I would like to create a map for the marginal occupancy probability of each species using that covariate across all my study sites (5).

I did this but I'm not sure if the equation for each species should only include the coefficients for their intersect and beta for the covariate, or if I should also include other coefficients. Or maybe I should do something entirely different.

load model —————————————————————

top <- readRDS(“top.rds”) ## top model
load covariates in model —————————————

cov <- read_csv(“site_covariates/site_covariates2.csv”)
sc <- scale(cov$flii_value1000) # only covariate for psi in top model
ct <- attr(sc, “scaled:center”) #7.85462
scc <- attr(sc, “scaled:scale”) #2.799441
ocelot ————————————-

## Because the covariate was centered in the model, I center it here too.

flii.s <- (flii_zam-ct)/scc

beta <- coef(top, type= “state”)

## beta[1] intersect of species 1

## beta[2] beta with covariate for species 1

## the rest of the coefficients are for the other species and their interactions

## I only worked with 1st and 2nd order parameters

logit.psi <- beta[1] + beta[2]*flii.s

psi <- exp(logit.psi)/(1+exp(logit.psi))

library(RColorBrewer)
cols = brewer.pal(9, “Greens”)

messages.subject: Q about a simulation study with occu in unmarked
messages.subject_clean: Q about a simulation study with occu in unmarked
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

With a colleague we are planning a simulation study to explore some features of the estimates of a simple static occupancy model as we vary the values of psi and p between 0.1 and 0.9. In some pilot runs with function occu()  in unmarked we have had quite a number of numerical failures where typically one or more SE’s in a model run were given as either NaN or an NA. We have tried to filter them out and rerun those cases.

There are two things we are unsure about:
We were wondering about some general criterion to diagnose a numerical failure, in particular also for those where the SE is estimated at some very large value (e.g., 10 or 100 or more) ?
We are also unsure whether repeating cases with numerical failures as just described is a good idea. After all, these will just be a feature of some combinations of the factors of our simulation (e.g., when psi or p are very small, leading to boundary estimates). Thus, it may be better to tally up the number of such numerical failures and report them as one of the results of our study ?

Thanks for comments and ideas.

Bestr regards  --- Marc

messages.subject: Re: Marginal occupancy map
messages.subject_clean: Marginal occupancy map
messages.body_plain:
Hi Gabby,

Since this model uses a multivariate bernoulli distribution for the response you can't calculate occupancy probability the way you would for a regular occupancy model. If you are interested in doing all the math yourself, I suggest looking at equations 1-3 of Rota 2016. Alternatively unmarked can do the work for you using predict().

To get the marginal occupancy for a given species under a given set of covariate values you would use commands something like:

newdata <- data.frame(flii.s=flii.s) # column name of covariate should exactly match name in model
pr <- predict(yourmodel, type="state", species="yourspecies", newdata=newdata)

Check out the help file for occuMulti for more examples of how to use predict.

Ken

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Use of ObsNum function in Unmarked
messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] Use of ObsNum function in Unmarked
messages.body_plain:
Dear Tristan,

I don't know what the ObsNum function is. But it should not be impossible to use an Nmix model (i.e., function pcount in unmarked) to estimate population size under the following two main assumptions:
You must be able to identify the individuals sufficiently well to exclude any double, triple .... counts of the same individual for a given occasion and trap. That is, a count such as, say, 5 must mean that there were exactly 5 unique individuals that appear in any number of photographs during the time period that you chose to define as an 'occasion'. You must be able to exclude the possibility that the first count was 4 individuals, of which one was photographed twice etc.
In addition, every detected individual must only occur at a single trap.
The main caveat then will be that your "abundance estimate" will in a sense still only be a sort of detection-corrected index, because the Nmix model is not a spatially explicit model. You don't know the areas associated with each trap, from which the observed individuals were drawn. Therefore, you will not be able to convert your abundance estimate into an estimate of density, or only under strong and untestable assumptions. Such as when you claim that all animals potentially detectable at a trap must come from some distance not further away than T, where T is chosen by you.

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Hi Marc,

Thank you very much for your reply.

As far as I understand it, ObsNum is total counts per camera trap and has been used in other posts as a site-level observation variable. I am just wondering whether including this in my model as a covariate of site-level observation isn't circular (I.e. higher detections at sites because counts are higher at those sites)?

For example:
pcount(~ObsNum ~ dist_to_road, UFO1)

Thanks for your help and time.

Kind regards,
Tristan

On Fri, 12 Nov 2021, 16:48 Marc Kery, <marc...@vogelwarte.ch> wrote:

> Dear Tristan,
>
> I don't know what the ObsNum function is. But it should not be impossible to use an Nmix model (i.e., function pcount in unmarked) to estimate population size under the following two main assumptions:
> You must be able to identify the individuals sufficiently well to exclude any double, triple .... counts of the same individual for a given occasion and trap. That is, a count such as, say, 5 must mean that there were exactly 5 unique individuals that appear in any number of photographs during the time period that you chose to define as an 'occasion'. You must be able to exclude the possibility that the first count was 4 individuals, of which one was photographed twice etc.
> In addition, every detected individual must only occur at a single trap.
> The main caveat then will be that your "abundance estimate" will in a sense still only be a sort of detection-corrected index, because the Nmix model is not a spatially explicit model. You don't know the areas associated with each trap, from which the observed individuals were drawn. Therefore, you will not be able to convert your abundance estimate into an estimate of density, or only under strong and untestable assumptions. Such as when you claim that all animals potentially detectable at a trap must come from some distance not further away than T, where T is chosen by you.
>
> Best regards  --- Marc
>
>
>
>

>
>
> data(mallard)
> mallardUMF <- unmarkedFramePCount(mallard.y, siteCovs = mallard.site,
> obsCovs = mallard.obs)
> (fm.mallard <- pcount(~ ivel+ date + I(date^2) ~ length + elev + forest, mallardUMF, K=30))
> (fm.mallard.nb <- pcount(~ date + I(date^2) ~ length + elev, mixture = "NB", mallardUMF, K=30))
> (fm1re <- ranef(fm1))
> plot(fm1re, subset=site %in% 1:25, xlim=c(-1,40))
> sum(bup(fm1re))         # Estimated population size
> sum(N)                  # Actual population size
>
> Thanks for your time and help.
>
> Kind regards,
> Tristan

messages.body_plain:
Dear Tristan,

If these total counts include the counts for the one species for which the Nmix model is run, then yes, this would be wrong, because circular. I think that if one wants to use the total count (btw, I assume this would be total number of pictures made during an occasion at a trap) as a detection covariate, then one would first have to subtract the number of pictures for the target species.

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Hi guys,

I'm not sure if this is related, but unmarked internally creates an observation covariate called 'obsNum' that you can include in the detection part of the model to get occasion-specific estimates of detection parameters (like model Mt in mark-recapture):

> library(unmarked)
> example(unmarked)
> occu(~obsNum ~1, umf)

Call:
occu(formula = ~obsNum ~ 1, data = umf)

Occupancy:
 Estimate    SE     z  P(>|z|)
     -1.1 0.231 -4.74 2.16e-06

Detection:
            Estimate    SE     z P(>|z|)
(Intercept)    0.235 0.403 0.584  0.5593
obsNum2        0.510 0.587 0.869  0.3847
obsNum3        0.164 0.573 0.286  0.7749
obsNum4        0.700 0.599 1.168  0.2428
obsNum5        1.407 0.676 2.081  0.0374

AIC: 275.2603

This isn't documented very well, and most people do this manually by creating a matrix to indicate the occasion number associated with each observation.

--
Richard Chandler
Associate Professor
Wildlife Ecology and Conservation
Warnell School of Forestry and Natural Resources
University of Georgia
762-499-4085
http://chandlerlab.uga.edu/

On Friday, 12 November 2021 at 20:15:21 UTC+2 rchandler wrote:
> Hi guys,
>
> I'm not sure if this is related, but unmarked internally creates an observation covariate called 'obsNum' that you can include in the detection part of the model to get occasion-specific estimates of detection parameters (like model Mt in mark-recapture):
>
> > library(unmarked)
> > example(unmarked)
> > occu(~obsNum ~1, umf)
>
> Call:
> occu(formula = ~obsNum ~ 1, data = umf)
>
> Occupancy:
>  Estimate    SE     z  P(>|z|)
>      -1.1 0.231 -4.74 2.16e-06
>
> Detection:
>             Estimate    SE     z P(>|z|)
> (Intercept)    0.235 0.403 0.584  0.5593
> obsNum2        0.510 0.587 0.869  0.3847
> obsNum3        0.164 0.573 0.286  0.7749
> obsNum4        0.700 0.599 1.168  0.2428
> obsNum5        1.407 0.676 2.081  0.0374
>
> AIC: 275.2603
>
>
> This isn't documented very well, and most people do this manually by creating a matrix to indicate the occasion number associated with each observation.
>
> --
> Richard Chandler
> Associate Professor
> Wildlife Ecology and Conservation
> Warnell School of Forestry and Natural Resources
> University of Georgia
> 762-499-4085
> http://chandlerlab.uga.edu/

> To: unma...@googlegroups.com <unma...@googlegroups.com>
> Subject: Re: [unmarked] Use of ObsNum function in Unmarked

> Dear Tristan,
>
> If these total counts include the counts for the one species for which the Nmix model is run, then yes, this would be wrong, because circular. I think that if one wants to use the total count (btw, I assume this would be total number of pictures made during an occasion at a trap) as a detection covariate, then one would first have to subtract the number of pictures for the target species.
>
> Best regards  --- Marc
>
> From: unma...@googlegroups.com <unma...@googlegroups.com> on behalf of Tristan Baird <u170...@tuks.co.za>

>

>
> As far as I understand it, ObsNum is total counts per camera trap and has been used in other posts as a site-level observation variable. I am just wondering whether including this in my model as a covariate of site-level observation isn't circular (I.e. higher detections at sites because counts are higher at those sites)?
>
> For example:
> pcount(~ObsNum ~ dist_to_road, UFO1)
>
> Thanks for your help and time.
>
> Kind regards,
> Tristan
>

> > Dear Tristan,
> >
> > I don't know what the ObsNum function is. But it should not be impossible to use an Nmix model (i.e., function pcount in unmarked) to estimate population size under the following two main assumptions:
> > You must be able to identify the individuals sufficiently well to exclude any double, triple .... counts of the same individual for a given occasion and trap. That is, a count such as, say, 5 must mean that there were exactly 5 unique individuals that appear in any number of photographs during the time period that you chose to define as an 'occasion'. You must be able to exclude the possibility that the first count was 4 individuals, of which one was photographed twice etc.
> > In addition, every detected individual must only occur at a single trap.
> > The main caveat then will be that your "abundance estimate" will in a sense still only be a sort of detection-corrected index, because the Nmix model is not a spatially explicit model. You don't know the areas associated with each trap, from which the observed individuals were drawn. Therefore, you will not be able to convert your abundance estimate into an estimate of density, or only under strong and untestable assumptions. Such as when you claim that all animals potentially detectable at a trap must come from some distance not further away than T, where T is chosen by you.
> >
> > Best regards  --- Marc

> >
> >

> >

> >
> >
> > data(mallard)
> > mallardUMF <- unmarkedFramePCount(mallard.y, siteCovs = mallard.site,
> > obsCovs = mallard.obs)
> > (fm.mallard <- pcount(~ ivel+ date + I(date^2) ~ length + elev + forest, mallardUMF, K=30))
> > (fm.mallard.nb <- pcount(~ date + I(date^2) ~ length + elev, mixture = "NB", mallardUMF, K=30))
> > (fm1re <- ranef(fm1))
> > plot(fm1re, subset=site %in% 1:25, xlim=c(-1,40))
> > sum(bup(fm1re))         # Estimated population size
> > sum(N)                  # Actual population size
> >
> > Thanks for your time and help.
> >
> > Kind regards,

messages.subject_clean: ranking det. covariates before incorporating psi covariates
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have a general question on methods in occupancy model formulation:

I've read several papers in which authors begin by ranking models with various covariates of detection, while holding occupancy constant. Then, after identifying a best-ranked detection model, this model is used to create subsequent models with the addition of covariates of occupancy.

I've also seen another method of simultaneously comparing models with varying covariates of both detection and occupancy.

First, is one method more advantageous than the other, and if so, why?

Second, is the former method still admissible if the best detection model has a low Akaike weight (e.g., other models of detection have a reasonable probability given the data)?

I've just ranked a set of 9 models just including covariates of detection. My plan was to rank models with occupancy covariates after finding the best-ranked detection model. However, my top model only has a weight of ~0.4, with 5 other models in the 95% confidence set. At this point, I'm unsure if it would be appropriate to continue with the top-ranked model, given that others may also be reasonable.

Thank you,
David

Dear all unmarked users,
I would like to raise a question. When I ran a single species occupancy model for red muntjac, I got a result showing that "distance to settlements" have a significant positive effect on detection probability and have a significant negative effect on occupancy probability. Is it normal or am I doing wrongly?
I would like to know why there is a contradictory effect of that covariate on detection and occupancy probability.
Thank you very much in advance.
Any answers, comments or suggestions are very grateful.

All the best,
AYE

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Can same environmental covariate have a different/opposite effect on occupancy and detection probability?
messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] Can same environmental covariate have a different/opposite effect on occupancy and detection probability?
messages.body_plain:
Dear AYE,

why should this be wrong ? The spatial distribution of your species and the factors that lead to detection or nondetection are two completely separate processes. Hence, a covariate may well have a positive effect on one and a negative on the other. I would rather say that such an "interaction" is quite interesting (I use this term though it is not technically one). So perhaps these muntjacs like being close to settlements because there they encounter fewer animal predators or more food, but at the same time they are afraid of us humans and hence must behave more secretively ?

More generally, the possibility of such opposite-sign effects is exactly one of the great strengths of hierarchical models such as the occupancy: by modeling the latent states separately from the observation process, they can tease apart these processes. In contrast, a detection-naive analysis (e.g., logistic regression, GAM, BRT, RF, ....) is only able to describe the compound effect of such a covariate on the "apparent occupancy". And that will then be really biased.

Back in 2008 I wrote a paper on this topic in the related context of the N-mixture model, see here: Kéry, M. 2008. Estimating abundance from bird counts: binomial mixture models uncover complex covariate relationships. The Auk 125: 336–345.

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.body_plain:
I've seen several papers use a detection-covariates-first approach to dealing with occupancy models when there are too many covariates to include every permutation of occupancy, detection, colonization, and extinction in a tractable way off the bat.  It's certainly an understandable and tractable approach, though it seems like there are some potential issues with it.

I think this paper is also relevant to the discussion.

Is your ad hoc model selection strategy affecting your multi-model inference?  Morin et al. 2020 Ecosphere.
https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdf/10.1002/ecs2.2997

Happy to hear others thoughts on all of the above as it's something I've grappled with in my own analyses.

-Alex

messages.body_plain:
Dear Alex,

that's a good cite there, thanks.

I recently re-read the Hooten & Hobbs Ecol.Mono.treatise on model selection and thought that an altogether different way to proceed might be a certain form of "regularization", where one fits a single model with all potentially interesting effects in there, but puts a prior on the coefficients (minus the intercepts). The more unimportant effects will then be shrunk towards zero more than the more important ones. Things to note would be:
you would normally have to do this in some BUGS software, i.e., go down the Bayesian road
I don't think that one could put a single prior on all coefficients when one has polynomial terms in there (e.g., elevation linear and squared) or interaction in addition to main effects of factors
And I would think that one would perhaps also put one prior on the coefficients of the occupancy and another on those of the detection model
Might be interesting to explore.

Best regards  -- Marc

messages.subject: Adding a certain covariate obliterates model psi estimates but decreases AIC?
messages.subject_clean: Adding a certain covariate obliterates model psi estimates but decreases AIC?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I’m attempting to rank a set of a-priori candidate occupancy models (single-season, single-species) and am having trouble understanding a pattern I’m seeing in my back-transformed occupancy estimates of certain models. If I add a certain covariate to any model, that model will rank significantly higher (lower AIC), but the psi estimate plummets to below 0.01.

For example:

In the below models, the DTNSP covariate is the covariate of interest...

Model1<- p(Midstory), psi(Grass+Midstory+DTNSP+Basal*Canopy)

Psi: 0.00523

AIC: 541.3877

When I remove DTNSP:

Model2<- p(Midstory), psi(Grass+Midstory+Basal*Canopy)

Psi: 0.736

AIC: 620.3784

What do you think is causing this and how do I address it?

For context, the covariate is distance to source population (0-160km). In my dataset, all occupied plots were close to source populations (<20km). However, although most unoccupied sites were >20km, there was a group that were extremely close to (now extinct) source populations (<1km). I’m wondering if these outliers in the unoccupied sites are causing this pattern.

Any help is appreciated!
Liam

Just wanted to note that tactically, I find this paper (doi.org/10.1002/jwmg.213 <https://doi.org/10.1002/jwmg.213>) helpful for defining a full model (to be fit and interpreted) or to help guide what level of complexity is tenable in any candidate models.

Also, to follow up on some of the regularization discussion, wanted to note that unmarked's occuPEN lets one try some of these approaches--the choice of penalty parameter/argument lambda for certain schemes has some direct analogy to placing a normal prior on the parameters (see text below eq 4. in Hutchinson et al.'s paper).  For this sort of concern, I guess the ridge or bayes penalties are probably more reasonable than the MPLE penalty (although I imagine many users would probably further prefer the Lasso). I often forget that unmarked fits this, but it strikes me that it would actually be useful for a lot of things and that maybe it should be far more commonly used. A ridge or bayes penalty seems reasonable for isotropic smoothing functions (e.g., 1d splines, spatial splines with a radial basis) or other things that might otherwise appear to require MCMC or other hard-coding. (I guess you'd have to use nonparboot for SE/CI, but I imagine this is no more time-consuming than even the fastest MCMC?)

John

Hi Alex,

Thanks for  your response! I did scale each continuous variable (including the one of interest) prior to fitting the models. I suppose I should have also included that I am using the linearComb function to backtransform my occupancy estimates. Perhaps I do not understand this function. Here is my linearComb code:

LC2<-linearComb(model18,coefficients=c(1,0,0,0,0,0,0),type='state')
backTransform(LC2)

I hold the intercept at 1 and each covariate at its mean (which in linearComb is represented by 0, if I am understanding this right). I have seen others use values other than "0" for their coefficients, and I'm unsure when it is appropriate to do so, or what value is represented by, say 0.5.

Interestingly, if I change my DTNSP coefficient to -1, the psi estimate for the same model skyrockets, but I do not know what "-1" represents (the minimum value of the covariate?):

LC2<-linearComb(model18,coefficients=c(1,0,0,-1,0,0,0),type='state')
backTransform(LC2)

Estimate: 0.939
SE: 0.0549
LinComb: 2.73

I have also been using the predict function to plot occupancy. E.g., predicting marginal effect of grass:

newdata = data.frame(
  Grass= seq(min(Grass),max(Grass), len=500),
  Midstory = rep(mean(Midstory),len=500),
  DTNSP =  rep(mean(Midstory),len=500)  ,
  BasalArea= rep(mean(BasalArea),len=500),
  CanopyHeight= rep(mean(CanopyHeight),len=500))

predicted<-predict(model18,type="state",newdata=newdata,appendData=T)

The plot <https://i.imgur.com/ocN8c6a.jpg> looks funky and the psi estimates are tiny.

However, if I hold DTNSP at its minimum value, check out how the plot changes <https://i.imgur.com/shsXJK3.jpg>. And the psi estimates are not super low anymore.

My conclusion is that because my occupied sites are <20km from a source population, holding the covariate at its mean (48.39 km on the normal scale) throws the psi estimates off because no occupied sites were anywhere above 20km from a source population.

I guess my question now is: is it appropriate to not hold DTNSP at its mean when estimating psi?

Thanks again,

Liam

messages.subject: Re: density vs abund & the ranking of global models
messages.subject_clean: density vs abund & the ranking of global models
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I thought I'd resurrect this thread. I'm currently facing a similar situation to what Auriel and Carly experienced. In ranking a set of single season occupancy models that just include covariates of detection, the most general model was the top ranked one. This seems to be a fairly uncommon situation, as I haven't found other cases of people describing this issue on the internet.

>From this thread, I've gathered that a general model being lowest-ranked in AIC might signal that the covariates being considered aren't informative.

Does anyone else have an opinion to add to Dan and Evan's discussion here, or know of any papers that describe this pattern and its cause in more detail?

Cheers,
David

On Tuesday, June 25, 2019 at 5:12:19 PM UTC-5 Dan Linden wrote:
> So glad to see this old thread resurrected.  :-D
>
> To clarify, Carly, your example does not suggest you've learned nothing.  It also does not suggest unexplained variation, as far as I can tell.  A few thoughts:
>
> 1) I recommend Andy and Marc's AHM book for a very accessible treatment on occupancy in unmarked and hierarchical modeling in general: Applied Hiearchical Modeling in Ecology <https://sites.google.com/site/appliedhierarchicalmodeling/home>
>
> 2) To be clear, all covariates in your example are detection covariates.  So you haven't learned anything about variation in occupancy there.  If your objectives relate to the detection process for some species, particularly if you are designing future monitoring, and/or you have no reason to think there is spatial variation in occurrence, this could make sense.
>
> 3) I stand by my comments that having the global model rank as the top model in an occupancy analysis is not a "problem".  I am certainly open to being shown otherwise.  This thread highlights nuance that goes way beyond occupancy or the unmarked package.
>
>
>
> On Monday, June 24, 2019 at 4:13:24 PM UTC-4, Carly Scott wrote:
> > Hi Dan,
> > As a novice unmarked user (and novice at modeling in general), this conversation was *slightly* hard for me to follow, so I just want to confirm what was settled on:
> >
> > If I have an sample model set:
> > 1) occu(~1~1, data=data) #null model
> > 2) occu(~%cover+trailtype+humanactivity+month~1, data=data) #global model
> > 3) occu(~%cover+trailtype~1, data=data) #subglobal
> > 4) occu(~%cover+month~1, data=data) #subglobal
> > etc etc...
> >
> > ...and if model 2 (global model) was ranked as the top model with AIC( chat ~1), then I haven't learned anything, correct?
> >
> > Does this mean that there is variation in my data that isn't explained by my covariates?
> > ...I'm just having a hard time interpreting this and figuring what I need to do to fix my models so that they are meaningful!
> >
> > I appreciate your help, your comments are always very useful for me!!
> >
> >
> > On Wednesday, March 11, 2015 at 9:47:35 PM UTC-4, Dan Linden wrote:
> > > Evan, I never presumed you didn't know what you were talking about.  That is why I made the Wayne's World comment - you are clearly an expert, there is no question.  I apologize for implying otherwise.  My intention was to focus the discussion because there are some differences with respect to the types of models fit in programs like PRESENCE and unmarked, vs. those typically fit in MARK (with some heavy overlap).  I know that you know all of this, again my comments are always with respect to unmarked users.
> > >
> > > Convenient for the sake of our discussion, we both approached my simple example from different angles.  I was not at all clear, but I envisioned the temperature covariate to be something that varied by time and space.  This is a typical situation where site is the sampling unit, as in an occupancy model.  It certainly does not apply when individual is the sampling unit, as in a mark-recapture model.  That critical detail makes all the difference here.
> > >
> > > So much of this material can be very confusing to the average user.  And it is hard to balance advocating rules of thumb vs. discouraging folks from relying on analysis recipes that sometimes lead to misguided decisions.  I guess what you hope is that people adequately familiarize themselves with the literature and seek expert opinions when possible.

> > > >
> > > > Psi: 0.00523
> > > >
> > > > AIC: 541.3877
> > > >
> > > > When I remove DTNSP:
> > > >
> > > > Model2<- p(Midstory), psi(Grass+Midstory+Basal*Canopy)
> > > >
> > > > Psi: 0.736
> > > >
> > > > AIC: 620.3784
> > > >
> > > > What do you think is causing this and how do I address it?
> > > >
> > > > For context, the covariate is distance to source population (0-160km). In my dataset, all occupied plots were close to source populations (<20km). However, although most unoccupied sites were >20km, there was a group that were extremely close to (now extinct) source populations (<1km). I’m wondering if these outliers in the unoccupied sites are causing this pattern.
> > > >
> > > > Any help is appreciated!
> > > > Liam

messages.subject: The new IPM textbook is out now !

messages.body_plain:
Dear colleagues,

it is our great pleasure to advertise the publication by Academic Press of our brand-new textbook on Integrated Population Models (IPMs), see cover attached. IPMs are an incredibly powerful framework for making the most of your data in population modeling, by fusing in a single statistical model multiple data sets on population counts and demographic quantities such as survival or productivity. In our book, we first give a comprehensive account of the theory of IPMs. In the second half, we then present a wide range of case studies that give a flavour of the tremendous power of these models to answer research questions and solve wildlife management problems. We provide vast amounts of very easily accessible code in R and JAGS, so we hope that the book, along with the associated resources, will kick-​start your own applications of IPMs.

You can get much more information on our book on the book website: www.vogelwarte.ch/ipm <http://www.vogelwarte.ch/ipm>. One of the bonus resources is a long document that you can download and which gives complete and richly commented code for the solutions to all the exercises in the book. In addition, you will find links to access all the code in the book on GitHub and to the R package IPMbook (available on CRAN), which contains useful functions and all data sets. Both the GitHub repo and the R package were created and are maintained by our colleague Mike Meredith (https://mmeredith.net/). Mike has been an invaluable help for the entire book project (see also book Acknowledgements) and is very warmly acknowledged.

Michael and Marc

messages.subject: Random effects in occu(): error in solve.default & error in optim
messages.subject_clean: Random effects in occu(): error in solve.default & error in optim
messages.body_plain:
Dear unmarked users

Together with a colleague, I am simulating detection/nondetection data for a single species and within one season under various combinations of true psi (occupancy probability) and true p (detection probability) for different habitat types.

We then want to fit an occupancy model using the function occu() from unmarked. Habitat is a categorical covariate on occupancy and we would like to fit it as a random effects factor. For each combination of true psi and true p, we simulate several datasets (5 for the moment, later it will be more). In some simulation replicates, the model-fitting works very well, but in some I get either of the following 3 errors:

1.Error in solve.default(full) :

system is computationally singular: reciprocal condition number = 1.05845e-46

2.Error in solve.default(full) :

Lapack routine dgesv: system is exactly singular: U[1,1] = 0

3.Error in optim(starts, fn = tmb_mod$fn, gr = tmb_mod$gr, method = method,:

gradient in optim evaluated to length 1 not 3

I suspect errors 1 and 2 are somehow related and that error 3 refers to an optimization gradient used by TMB to find the MLE…?

I have tried to manipulate the initial values in order to be closer to the true values by setting the intercept inits to either 0.25 or 0.75 (depending on whether the true value is > 0.5 or < 0.5). I also set the initial value for the sd of the random effect to some value between 0.3 and 1 to avoid extremely small inits for sd, but this did not solve the problem, errors still keep occurring. I nevertheless believe the problem is related to the initial values because when I encounter an error and try to manipulate the inits manually, I always end up finding some inits that work for that simulated dataset. But I have not found a set of inits that would work for the entire simulation (i.e. for all combinations of true psi and p values and for all 5-100 simulation replicates of each of those combinations).

Does anybody know what it is that leads to these specific error messages and how I can avoid them?

Thank you in advance for any input. The code is below.

Best wishes

Gesa

Code & notes:

Function simOccFac() serves to simulate the dataset. It results in detection histories (1/0) for M sites and J=2 visits where sites are sampled from 5 different habitats. The simulation of the dataset is repeated if 1) there are no detections at all, 2) the species was detected during at all sites during all visits, or 3) not all habitats were sampled.

simrep <- 5  # number of simulation replicates

M <- 200     # number of sites

pvals <- seq(0.1, 0.4, 0.1)  # levels of true psi and p to be tested

for(i in 1:length(pvals)){     # Loop over levels of psi

  for(j in 1:length(pvals)){   # Loop over levels of p

    cat(paste('\n*** Doing psi =', pvals[i], 'and p =', pvals[j], '***'))

    for(k in 1:simrep){

      repeat{

        # simulate data set

        dat <- simOccFac(M=M, J=2, mean.occupancy=pvals[i],

                         mean.detection=pvals[j],

                         nHab=5, range.HAB=4)

        # conditions to retain dataset: at least 1 detection; at least 1 site with < 2 detections; all factor levels occur

        if(sum(dat$y) > 0 & sum(dat$y) < 2*M & sum(table(dat$HAB)>0)==5){

          break

        }

      }

      # create unmarked dataframe

      umf <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y=dat$y,

                               siteCovs=data.frame(habitat=as.factor(dat$HAB)))

      # provide starting values

      int <- c(qlogis(runif(1)), runif(1),  # occupancy parameters: psi-intercept (mean), sd of random effect

               qlogis(runif(1)))            # detection parameters: p-intercept

      # int <- c(qlogis(ifelse(pvals[i]<0.5, 0.25, 0.75)), runif(1, 0.3, 1),

               # qlogis(ifelse(pvals[j]<0.5, 0.25, 0.75)))

      # fit model

      fm <- occu(~1 ~ (1|habitat), data=umf, starts=int, control=list(maxit=1000))

    }

  }

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Estimating abundance from acoustic data
messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] Estimating abundance from acoustic data
messages.body_plain:
We faced this same problem with double-counting in bats and N-mixture, using Royle's model in our counts at Mammoth Cave, which have not yet been published. We developed a workaround for the problem, but I can't imagine how it could be applied to acoustic data (ours are images at emergence). There are some Bayesian abundance models of Kery's that could accommodate double-counting. Double-counting is treated as an allocation error (false positive) in these. On the other hand, you might consider using Royle's abundance dependent occupancy or that of Miller (which is robust to allocation error). Both are implemented in unmarked. If you have a lot of data and are working at regional scales, these might work for you. You lose some information by reducing the counts to occupancy, but they are fairly robust to violations that sink N-mixture.

Tom Ingersoll, PhD
Mathematician

On Friday, November 26, 2021, 09:52:29 AM EST, Carlos Henrique Russi <carlosh...@gmail.com> wrote:

Hi everyone.

I'm developing a project whose objective is to estimate the abundance (correcting for detectability) of bats at different elevations and seasons. For sampling, I will use ultrasound recorders, which will be installed at each location for 6 consecutive nights in each season of the year (summer, autumn, etc.), resulting in 24 nights of sampling per location (6 nights * 4 seasons).

In my view, the Dail and Mansen N-mixture open population model (pcountOpen function) would be the natural alternative to analyze such data, as it would allow me to model both the initial abundance of each location and the population dynamics throughout the year.

However, my data has a problem that I believe cannot be detected by such models: the same bat will certainly be detected numerous times in the same night. Through my data it is impossible to distinguish if, for example, 10 records come from 10 individuals detected once each, or only 1 individual detected 10 times.

In this context, my questions are:
(1) Am I right in thinking that the Dail and Mansen model is not capable of dealing with such a problem?
(2) Are there any alternatives in unmarked package to model abundance and detectability when an (unmarked) individual can be detected multiple times in the same sample?

--

messages.subject_clean: Random effects in occu(): error in solve.default & error in optim
messages.body_plain:
I think you have diagnosed this correctly. I've seen all three of these types of optimization errors and I haven't been able to sort out exactly which conditions lead to each one. I'm not sure it matters since the solution, as you note, is either to examine the data or the initial values or both.

I've found that with sparse presence/absence datasets unmarked-TMB can have a very hard time getting good estimates for random effects, especially compared to considering the covariate as a fixed effect instead. I suspect there is not a single set of initial values that will solve optimization problems in all cases (if there was we should be using them as the defaults!). Given your simulation inputs, with J=2, it looks like you are probably generating some pretty sparse datasets (e.g. when p=0.1 and psi=0.1). It looks like you have some checks to reject certain datasets, which is good. However, realistically, you are probably not going to be able to fit the model with 1 (or even a handful) of detections, even without the random effect. So, you might want to adjust those checks to require more detections. You may also want to check not only whether all levels of HAB occur in the dataset but also whether some HAB levels have no detections at all as I suspect that could also cause optimization problems.

Also you mention psi/p > 0.5 but it doesn't seem like the simulation procedure creates any datsets like that currently, but maybe I'm missing something  (pval=seq(0.1,0.4,0.1))

Ken

Dear Ken

Thank you for your good idea to make even stronger conditions to retain a dataset, I will try out your 2 suggestions.
I wonder, however, whether it may not introduce some bias into the estimates if I only retain datasets that contain > n detections (whether n is 3 or 4 or whatever) because this might force the average number of detections to be too high with respect to the true psi/p value (e.g. in case of psi=0.1 and p=0.1). Similarly, I believe forcing all habitat types to have at least one detection would remove samples where some habitat would be highly unfavorable for the species, also creating some sort of bias... Could not this happen?
I will try your suggestions in any case. I was also told that the ubms-package might be more capable of dealing with these type of low-number-of-detections data. That would be my next option then if I cannot get it to work like this.

You are actually right, the code includes only pvals between 0.1 and 0.4, so the statement psi/p>0.5 does not apply here really. I used these pvals as my try-out settings only. Later (i.e. when the try-out settings work without error), I will run pvals between 0.1 and 0.9 at quite small intervals of 0.02 or 0.05.

Best wishes
Gesa

messages.body_plain:
Yes, I'd agree that it is not ideal to have to discard simulated datasets, and if you remove additional datasets you risk overestimating the ability of the model to recover parameter estimates (since you are ignoring the most challenging scenarios). Perhaps you could keep all simulated datasets and then keep track of both the accuracy of the estimates (for models you are able to successfully fit) and the proportion of simulations for which you were able to actually get the model to run, and use those two pieces of information together. I guess it depends on the goals of the simulation exercise.

Ken

Say that I want to use Forested Area (numeric variable; FA) in my occupancy model (for the sake of this example, let's assume that detection is constant). I have seen that it can be computed as occu(~1, ~FA, unmarkedFrameOccu object) .

Now, say that I want to use all the possible combinations of my 6 variables to run my occupancy model. I could add them up manually, but that would take a while. So, my question is if there is a way to do it automatically, by providing a list of my variables(?).

Thanks in advance!!

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Number of covariate combinations
messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] Number of covariate combinations
messages.body_plain:
Using a canned (and thoroughly tested) function is usually the way to go (such as the approach that Marc suggested).

However, here is one (not thoroughly tested) approach for running the analysis for all possible subsets:

# Create some fake data
  y = matrix(rbinom(100,1,0.2), ncol=2)
  umf = unmarkedFrameOccu(y=y,
    siteCovs=data.frame(a=rnorm(50), b=rnorm(50), c=rnorm(50)))

# Generate all possible models
  variables = c("a", "b", "c")
  n <- length(variables)
  results = list()
  for (i in 1:(2^n-1)) {
      v <- as.logical(intToBits(i))[1:n]
      occu.formula = as.formula(paste("~ 1 ~", paste(variables[v], collapse=" + ")))
      results[[i]] = occu(occu.formula, umf)
  }

Then you can process the results object (ranking by AIC, etc.).

I also don't want the opportunity to go by for commenting on "testing my variables for multicollinearity".  While it is important to know your data intimately, throwing out highly  correlated variables really just "ignores" multicollinearity and doesn't fix the issue.  Removing correlated variables might certainly be necessary if there are numerical convergence problems. But if you are just needing predictions or the variables are simply what a decision maker has available, then unless you have zillions of predictors, you might not want to toss any when fitting.

But if the objective is learning about the effect of predictors (as opposed to making predictions as the major objective), then your knowledge is essential as to how to proceed (as opposed to some automatic tossing of highly correlated variables).  If you don't have the knowledge (outside of what's in the data), then having highly correlated variables is more than problematic with such an objective.

Jim

messages.subject_clean: AW: [unmarked] Response variable distribution assumptions?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Vlad,

OH YES !

Typical assumptions are Bernoulli for detection/nondetection (a.k.a., “presence/absence”) data and something like a Poisson, zero-inflated Poisson, Negative Binomial, zero-inflated NB, Conway-Maxwell Poisson or some other discrete-valued distribution for counts (a.k.a., “abundance data”). Not all of those are implemented in unmarked though.

Best regards  -- Marc
